Palladium-catalyzed aminoalkynylation/
alleneamination of urea-tethered alkenes: access
to imidazolidinones bearing alkynes and allenes
Qianqian Hu,†<sup>a</sup> Cangzhu Hu,†<sup>a</sup> Tian Tang,<sup>a</sup> Qing Wu,<sup>a</sup> Weiming Hu, *<sup>b</sup>
Qiang Dai *<sup>c</sup> and Lei Wang *<sup>a</sup>

A novel palladium-catalyzed aminoalkynylation/alleneamination of
urea-tethered alkenes has been developed, ofering an eficient strat-
egy for the synthesis of imidazolidinones bearing alkynes and allenes in
moderate to good yields. The reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope,
excellent functional group tolerance and good synthetic versatility.
Imidazolidinones represent an important class of heterocyclic
compounds, which are widely found in numerous natural
products, bioactive molecules, and pharmacologically relevant
agents.<sup>1,2</sup> In addition to their biological significance, imidazo-
lidinones play a crucial role in synthetic organic chemistry as
valuable intermediates for the construction of more complex and
functionalized molecules. Owing to their structural diversity and
potential for distinct biological activities, the development ofeficient
synthetic methodologies for imidazolidinone frameworks has gar-
nered considerable attention over the past two decades.<sup>3–5</sup> Among
the established strategies, transition metal-catalyzed diamination of
di-tert-butyldiaziridinone has been extensively explored for the con-
struction of these key imidazolidinone scaffolds (Scheme 1a).<sup>5</sup> Alter-
natively, the 1,2-diamination of ureas has emerged as an attractive
approach for the synthesis of imidazolidinones.<sup>6–8</sup> For example,
Gong and co-workers reported a Pd(II)-catalyzed asymmetric 1,2-
diamination of 1,3-dienes with ureas, enabling access to a variety
of enantioenriched imidazolidinone derivatives (Scheme 1b(I)).<sup>7</sup> Sub-
sequently, Lin and Yao developed a novel Pd-catalyzed sequential
hydroamination of 1,3-enynes with diverse ureas, affording
aminomethyl-substituted allenes, which then underwent cyclization
to yield a broad range of imidazolidinones (Scheme 1b(II)).<sup>8</sup> Despite
these notable advances, the development of more efficient, selective,
and broadly applicable synthetic methods for imidazolidinone con-
struction remains highly desirable.
The direct difunctionalization of alkenes has emerged as a
powerful and eficient strategy for the straightforward construction
of complex molecular architectures.<sup>9</sup> Over the past few decades,
palladium-catalyzed carboheterofunctionalization of alkenes has
been extensively developed as a general and efective approach for
the synthesis of nitrogen-containing heterocycles.<sup>10,11</sup> Despite sig-
nificant progress, these methodologies have largely been limited to
the incorporation of aryl or alkenyl groups, highlighting the need
for broader functional group diversity. Palladium-catalyzed ami-
noalkynylation of alkenes remains a significant synthetic chal-
lenge, with only a limited number of strategies reported to date.

A novel palladium-catalyzed aminoalkynylation/alleneamination of
urea-tethered alkenes has been developed, ofering an eficient strat-
egy for the synthesis of imidazolidinones bearing alkynes and allenes in
moderate to good yields. The reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope,
excellent functional group tolerance and good synthetic versatility.
Imidazolidinones represent an important class of heterocyclic
compounds, which are widely found in numerous natural
products, bioactive molecules, and pharmacologically relevant
agents.<sup>1,2</sup> In addition to their biological significance, imidazo-
lidinones play a crucial role in synthetic organic chemistry as
valuable intermediates for the construction of more complex and
functionalized molecules. Owing to their structural diversity and
potential for distinct biological activities, the development ofeficient
synthetic methodologies for imidazolidinone frameworks has gar-
nered considerable attention over the past two decades.<sup>3–5</sup> Among
the established strategies, transition metal-catalyzed diamination of
di-tert-butyldiaziridinone has been extensively explored for the con-
struction of these key imidazolidinone scaffolds (Scheme 1a).<sup>5</sup> Alter-
natively, the 1,2-diamination of ureas has emerged as an attractive
approach for the synthesis of imidazolidinones.<sup>6–8</sup> For example,
Gong and co-workers reported a Pd(II)-catalyzed asymmetric 1,2-
diamination of 1,3-dienes with ureas, enabling access to a variety
of enantioenriched imidazolidinone derivatives (Scheme 1b(I)).<sup>7</sup> Sub-
sequently, Lin and Yao developed a novel Pd-catalyzed sequential
hydroamination of 1,3-enynes with diverse ureas, affording
aminomethyl-substituted allenes, which then underwent cyclization
to yield a broad range of imidazolidinones (Scheme 1b(II)).<sup>8</sup> Despite
these notable advances, the development of more efficient, selective,
and broadly applicable synthetic methods for imidazolidinone con-
struction remains highly desirable.
The direct difunctionalization of alkenes has emerged as a
powerful and eficient strategy for the straightforward construction
of complex molecular architectures.<sup>9</sup> Over the past few decades,
palladium-catalyzed carboheterofunctionalization of alkenes has
been extensively developed as a general and efective approach for
the synthesis of nitrogen-containing heterocycles.<sup>10,11</sup> Despite sig-
nificant progress, these methodologies have largely been limited to
the incorporation of aryl or alkenyl groups, highlighting the need
for broader functional group diversity. Palladium-catalyzed ami-
noalkynylation of alkenes remains a significant synthetic chal-
lenge, with only a limited number of strategies reported to date.
For instance, Waser and co-workers developed an intriguing
intramolecular aminoalkynylation of alkenes using ethynylbenzio-
doxolone (EBX) or alkyl-substituted alkynyl bromides, enabling the
synthesis of valuable alkyne-functionalized aza-heterocycles.<sup>12,13</sup>
More recently, Carreira’s group disclosed a distinctive Pd-cata-
lyzed aminoalkynylation of highly substituted alkenes facilitated
by picolinamide directing groups and iodoalkynes to aford a
diverse array of alkynylated pyrrolidines.<sup>13</sup> Despite these advances,
further development of new methodologies and their application
to synthetically relevant scafolds remain highly desirable. In this
context, we have developed an eficient Pd-catalyzed aminoalkyny-
lation of urea-tethered alkenes with alkynyl bromides, afording
alkynyl-functionalized imidazolidinones (Scheme 1c). In addition,
we have successfully achieved a Pd-catalyzed alleneamination of
urea-linked alkenes with propargylic acetates, providing access to
imidazolidinones bearing allene moieties (Scheme 1c).

With the optimized conditions in hand, the scope of the
aminoalkynylation was first assessed by employing a range of
urea-linked alkenes 1 with (bromoethynyl)benzene 2a as the cou-
pling partner (Scheme 2). Specifically, a range of aryl rings attached
to the nitrogen atom in urea were first discussed. Electron-donating
groups such as methyl and methoxyl, and electron-withdrawing
groups like fluoro, chloro and bromo groups were well tolerated,
delivering the corresponding products (3b–3f) in 79–98% yields.
Additionally, the configuration of 3b was confirmed by X-ray
diffraction.<sup>14</sup> Particularly, some strong electron-withdrawing groups
were also well tolerated, and the trifluoromethyl- and cyano-group
substitution products 3g and 3h were afforded with high yields
(88% and 91%). Notably, the ortho-methyl substituted substrate
proceeded smoothly, but product 3j was obtained in relatively lower
yield (34%). This result indicated that the steric effect could not be
ignored. The disubstituted substrate also exhibits excellent reaction
activity, and product 3k was formed in 94% yield. In addition, the
benzyl group was also well tolerated, and the corresponding
product 3l was delivered in 46% yield. Remarkably, replacing
the methyl group with the benzene ring in the substrate had no
negative effect on the reaction, and product 3m was isolated in a
good yield of 83%. Meanwhile, disubstituted alkene substrates
were also good reaction partners as products 3n and 3o bearing a
quaternary carbon center were obtained in 71% and 58% yields.
To further explore the substrate scope, various bromoacety-
lenes 2 were subjected to the standard reaction conditions to react
with 1-allyl-1-methyl-3-phenylurea 1b (Scheme 3). As expected,
reaction of aryl alkynyl bromides proceeded smoothly to give
the corresponding products in moderate to good yields (4a–4g,
4i–4k, 86–95%). Notably, the cyano-substituted aromatic
bromoacetylene showed a lower reactivity, and product 4h was
obtained only in 18% yield. In addition, alkynyl bromides contain-
ing heterocyclic, cyclic alkenyl and cyclic alkyl bromides were all
compatible to deliver 4l, 4m, 4n and 4o in 38%, 75%, 79% and
67%, respectively. The alkyl substituted alkynyl bromides such as
tert-butyl-, n-pentyl-, and n-hexyl-were also applicable, and the
corresponding products 4q–4s were obtained in 55%–92% yields.

Allenes are important motifs for drugs and bioactive natural
products.<sup>15</sup> Next, we proceeded to explore a range of urea-linked
alkenes 1 with propargylic acetates 5 for the synthesis of imidazo-
lidones bearing allenes (Scheme 4). Again, both electron-donating
and electron-withdrawing groups such as Me-, OMe-, Cl- and CN-
bearing aryl rings attached to the nitrogen atom in urea were well
tolerated, yielding the corresponding products 6a–6e in moderate
to good yields (52–79%). Furthermore, various propargylic acetates
also reacted well regardless of the electrostatic effect and the steric
hindrance effect, which provided a range of imidazolidones bearing
allene derivatives 6f–6s in good yields (24–83%). Particularly, the
substrate bearing a trimethylsilyl group formed the target product
6m in a low yield of 29%, which demonstrated the good compat-
ibility of this method to some extent.
To further prove the practicality of this approach, the reaction
between 1b and 2a was successfully scaled up to a 4.5 mmol scale,
and product 3b was isolated in 1.0 g with an acceptable yield of 73%
(Scheme 5a). Versatile transformations of 3b were also successfully
carried out (Scheme 5b); 3b underwent TfOH cyclization to aford
seven-membered N-heterocycle 7. Then, the carbon–carbon tri-
ple bond and the carbonyl group were reduced, and products 8
and 9 were delivered in 70% and 49% yields, respectively.
